messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel was 34, a married firefighter with the kind of broad-shouldered, controlled manner that made it easy to miss how much effort it took him to stay composed. He first began to change after a deployment as a relief worker in a war zone, where the work that had drawn on his training also stripped away any ordinary sense of safety. He had been moving through damaged streets and temporary shelters, helping with evacuations and supplies, when the threat was no longer abstract but immediate: unknown people appearing at doorways, sudden movements in crowds, and the constant need to know where the nearest exit was if shells fell again or a route closed unexpectedly. He later described those weeks as teaching him to live with one eye always fixed on escape. What stayed with him most was not a single image but the feeling that survival depended on never letting himself settle.

When he returned home, Daniel expected relief, but his body and mind behaved as if the war zone had followed him back. He found himself scanning exits the moment he entered a room, taking in windows, hallways, and doorways before he could listen to anyone speaking. Even inside his own home he felt on guard, alert to the slightest unfamiliar sound or interruption, as if danger could step in without warning. In ordinary places he felt threatened by strangers approaching him, especially if someone came up quickly in a parking lot, at the grocery store, or near the firehouse while he was off duty. He could not shake the sense that if he failed to notice the wrong person at the wrong moment, something terrible would happen before he had time to react.

Over the following months, Daniel quietly built a life around keeping that fear from rising any higher. He made sure to stay close to the exit whenever he sat in a restaurant, in church, or at his son’s school events, and he chose seats and parking spots with escape routes in mind. He stopped exercising in the way he used to, telling himself he was too busy, though what he did not say was that sustained exertion left him feeling trapped in his own body, too keyed up to trust that he would be able to get away if he needed to. He also found himself pushing away positive feelings when they appeared. Moments of warmth with his wife, pride after a good shift, or the easy happiness of playing with his children could suddenly feel unsafe, almost like a lure into lowering his guard. Rather than let himself relax, he would cut those feelings off quickly, as though joy made him careless and carelessness invited danger.

At first these habits seemed sensible to him, even protective. He told himself that staying near exits and avoiding exercise kept him ready, that not getting too comfortable prevented him from being caught off guard. But the cost was that his world shrank around the very precautions meant to preserve it. The more he arranged his days around escape and vigilance, the less able he felt to believe he was truly safe anywhere. Ordinary spaces became loaded with menace because he was always measuring how quickly he could get out, and strangers seemed more alarming because his attention was trained so hard on possible threat. Even at home, where nothing objectively dangerous was happening, he remained braced, listening for the shift in the air that might mean trouble.

By the time he came to treatment, Daniel was exhausted by the constant effort of keeping himself on alert. His wife had noticed how he would hover near doors at family gatherings, decline exercise with the children, and withdraw the moment a good mood started to break through. He had finally agreed to seek help after realizing that his life in the firehouse, at home, and in the ordinary spaces between had become organized around fear rather than around the work and family he valued. What he was most afraid of was that if he let himself relax, even for a moment, he would miss the danger and lose control. What he was most hoping for was to feel safe enough to stay in a room, breathe normally, and be with his family without constantly searching for the way out.
